entries.t: The Diabetic Whose Sugar Looked Fine
entries.x: The Diabetic Whose Sugar Looked Fine A real ED presentation, worked through one step at a time. Make the calls as you go — then read exactly what happened, and where the real team nearly got it wrong. Dotted, colored terms — like this — show a quick definition on hover or tap.

The Patient 28F · Emergency Department One week of polyuria, polydipsia, poor appetite, and vomiting. Background: type 2 diabetes that started as gestational diabetes eight years ago, obesity, and a prior admission for severe hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis — a detail that's going to matter later, since it puts a second, unrelated diagnosis on the table before she's even triaged. Metformin Biguanide — reduces hepatic glucose output; usually first-line for T2DM Glipizide Sulfonylurea — stimulates the pancreas to release more insulin Dapagliflozin (SGLT2i) SGLT2 inhibitor — blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney, independent of insulin. The key player in this case. Atorvastatin Statin — lowers LDL cholesterol by blocking HMG-CoA reductase Gemfibrozil Fibrate — lowers triglycerides via PPAR-alpha activation Five drugs, three different diseases. Before a single vital sign is taken, that medication list alone tells you this history is doing a lot of the diagnostic work — hover each one if a class doesn't ring a bell.

How She Got Here The Lead-Up She took her dapagliflozin SGLT2 inhibitor — blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney, independent of insulin as usual again this morning — "didn't want my sugars to spike." None of these four events looks dramatic in isolation. Stacked together — a chronic SGLT2 inhibitor, a recent infection, and days of poor intake — they're the textbook setup for exactly the diagnosis that's easiest to miss.

On Arrival Vitals & Exam HR 104 BP 108/68 RR 24 Temp 36.9°C SpO₂ 98% Glucose (mg/dL) 111 Exam: dry oral mucosa. Abdomen soft, non-tender , no guarding — an important negative given her history of pancreatitis, and one worth registering consciously rather than skimming past. How an EM Physician Reads This Tachycardia plus tachypnea with a normal oxygen saturation in a diabetic patient should trigger one specific mental branch: is this simple volume depletion, or is it respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis? The two can look similar on a monitor. The tell is usually the character of the breathing — deep and regular ( Kussmaul Deep, rapid breathing that compensates for metabolic acidosis by blowing off CO₂ respirations) points toward acidosis; shallow and rapid points more toward pain, fever, or anxiety. Either way, this vital sign pattern by itself is reason enough to send a gas before settling on a diagnosis — not after.

Approach & Review Reading Any Vitals Panel This is the systematic scan worth running on every vitals panel, not just this one — keep it in your back pocket. 1 Pair them physiologically, not in isolation. HR + BP together for circulation; RR + SpO₂ together for ventilation and oxygenation. 2 Ask what's compensating for what. A fast HR or RR is rarely the primary problem — it's usually the body correcting for volume loss, acidosis, pain, or fever. 3 A normal number doesn't mean a normal system. SpO₂ 98% only confirms oxygenation — it says nothing about ventilation or acid-base status. 4 Turn the pattern into a short differential before reaching for a single diagnosis or a single test. 5 Re-check vitals after every intervention. A repeat set is itself a diagnostic test — it tells you whether your working diagnosis is actually correct.

Checkpoint Before Any Labs Come Back Take thirty seconds and actually write something down before you look at the labs — the exercise only works if you commit to an answer first. What's on your differential for a diabetic with a week of polyuria, polydipsia, poor appetite, and vomiting? Compare against a broad differential Worth having on the list: diabetic (euglycemic) ketoacidosis, starvation ketosis, gastroenteritis/dehydration, an occult infection, and — given her history — hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis. Nobody's checked a glucose yet, so DKA has to stay on the list on history alone. Notice that "her glucose is probably fine, she's on a good regimen" isn't a reason to drop it — that assumption is exactly what this case is going to test.

Knowledge Check Definitions Matter "Euglycemic DKA" is classically defined as ketoacidosis with a blood glucose below roughly: 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL) 11.1 mmol/L (200 mg/dL) 13.9 mmol/L (250 mg/dL) 16.7 mmol/L (300 mg/dL) The "classic" DKA threshold most people memorize (13.9 mmol/L / 250 mg/dL) describes hyperglycemic DKA. Euglycemic DKA is defined well below that — which is exactly what makes it easy to miss if the number is the first thing you check rather than the last.

Lab Interpretation First Bloodwork Glucose 111 mg/dL (6.2 mmol/L) · anion gap Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻); estimates unmeasured acids in the blood. Normal is roughly 8–12. 20 · HbA1c Glycated hemoglobin — reflects average blood glucose over the prior ~3 months 10% · lipase normal. What Actually Jumps Out Scanning a panel like this, an EM physician's eye goes to the gap before the glucose. A gap of 20 with a pH of 7.27 is a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, full stop — that's true no matter what the glucose says. The glucose only tells you which flavor of ketoacidosis you might be dealing with, not whether one exists at all. Getting that order backwards — anchoring on the glucose first, gap second — is exactly how euglycemic DKA gets missed on a busy shift.

Approach & Review Reading Any Blood Gas The same five-step read applies whether it's a VBG, an ABG, or any panel with a pH and an anion gap on it. 1 Look at the pH first. Acidemic (<7.35) or alkalemic (>7.45)? That tells you which direction the primary process is pushing. 2 Find the primary disturbance. Whichever value — pCO₂ or HCO₃⁻ — moves in the same direction as the pH abnormality is the primary problem. 3 Check compensation. Is the other system responding by roughly the expected amount? If not, a second primary disorder is layered on top. 4 If it's a metabolic acidosis, calculate the anion gap. Na⁺ − (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻). Above roughly 12 means unmeasured acids are present. 5 Run the gap differential. High gap: ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, toxic alcohols, uremia, salicylates. Normal gap: GI bicarbonate losses or renal tubular acidosis. 6 Never let a reassuring glucose skip step 4. The gap and the ketones are what actually confirm or exclude DKA — not the glucose.

Checkpoint Does This Rule Out DKA? Glucose is 111 mg/dL. Bicarbonate 18, anion gap 20, pH 7.27. Does the normal-looking glucose rule out DKA? Yes — DKA requires hyperglycemia by definition No — an elevated gap and acidosis can occur without marked hyperglycemia, especially on an SGLT2 inhibitor No, but only because her creatinine is also abnormal Yes, unless serum ketones are checked first Hyperglycemia is part of the textbook triad, not a hard requirement written into anyone's physiology. The acidosis and ketosis are the dangerous parts; the glucose is just the number most people check first out of habit.

The Twist The Working Diagnosis The admitting team's call: starvation ketosis . She'd barely eaten for three days — same anion gap, more comfortable label. It's not an unreasonable first guess. It's just not a complete one. Settling on an early diagnosis and reading every later finding through that lens is a classic example of: Availability bias Anchoring bias Confirmation bias Premature closure All four are real, related diagnostic-error concepts — anchoring specifically means the first impression keeps coloring how new data gets read, even as that data accumulates. Building In a Check One habit that catches cases like this: before signing off on any diagnosis, ask whether it explains every abnormal number in front of you, not just the convenient ones. "Starvation ketosis" explains mild ketones. It does not comfortably explain an anion gap of 20 or a pH of 7.27 — simple starvation is typically a mild, well-compensated acidosis, nowhere near this degree of derangement. When the numbers don't fully fit the label, the usual answer is that the label is wrong, not the numbers.

Lab Interpretation Six Hours Later Glucose 111 → 186 mg/dL Rising, but still nowhere near the "classic" DKA cutoff Anion Gap 20 → 21 Not improving on "starvation" management Bicarbonate 18 → 16 mmol/L Getting worse, not better A single lab value is a photograph; two lab values, six hours apart, are a movie. On its own, a gap of 21 barely looks different from 20 — but paired with a falling bicarbonate despite treatment for the wrong diagnosis, it says the underlying process is still fully active. Whenever a patient isn't trending the way your working diagnosis predicts, that's the system telling you to revisit the diagnosis before reaching for more of the same plan.

entries.t: Reading a Repeat Set of Labs
entries.x: Approach & Review Reading a Repeat Set of Labs A single value is a snapshot. This is how to read the second one. 1 Never interpret one value in isolation once a repeat exists. Direction matters as much as magnitude. 2 Ask: does this trend fit my working diagnosis and treatment? If the patient isn't responding the way the diagnosis predicts, one of the two is wrong. 3 Separate "not better yet" from "actively worse." A flat gap 30 minutes into fluids is different from a widening gap six hours into treatment. 4 Re-anchor if the trajectory doesn't fit. This is usually the moment a missed diagnosis gets caught — if it's going to be caught at all. 5 Don't let one reassuring number carry the whole picture. A slowly rising glucose means nothing if the gap and pH are moving the wrong way.

Checkpoint Time to Confirm It The anion gap hasn't budged in six hours of "starvation" management. What single test would directly confirm ketoacidosis? Check β-hydroxybutyrate The dominant ketone body produced during DKA — a direct, quantitative marker of ongoing ketogenesis is the ketone body that actually predominates in DKA, more so than acetoacetate — which is the only one a standard urine dipstick detects. That mismatch matters twice: a dipstick can underestimate true ketosis, and can even look worse as a patient improves, since treatment converts β-hydroxybutyrate back into acetoacetate. A direct serum level sidesteps both problems, which is why it — not a urine dip — is the test to send and to trend. Hers came back at 5.29 mmol/L — markedly elevated (normal is under roughly 0.6 mmol/L). But getting there wasn't simple: her triglycerides had peaked at 2050 mg/dL, and the sample kept hemolyzing from the lipemia. The lab had to spin it down and remove the fatty layer before the ketone level could even be measured. Real labs don't always cooperate with the algorithm — knowing that a "pending" or "unable to process" result can itself be a clinical clue is part of the job.

Mechanism Why the Glucose Lied SGLT2 inhibitors work by dumping glucose into the urine — independent of insulin. That lowers blood sugar without fixing the actual problem: insulin is still relatively deficient, glucagon still dominates, and fat keeps getting broken down into ketone bodies. The two arms of this diagram run in parallel and don't know about each other — that's the whole reason the glucose can look reassuring while the acid-base picture quietly deteriorates. (See the glucose-lowering drugs lecture for how the rest of this drug class behaves.)

Knowledge Check Beyond This Case Besides infection and reduced intake, which is also a well-documented trigger for SGLT2-inhibitor euglycemic DKA? NSAID use Perioperative fasting / surgery Starting a beta-blocker A high-protein diet This is exactly why surgical teams are now told to hold SGLT2 inhibitors for several days before elective procedures — fasting plus surgical stress reproduces the same low-insulin, low-intake setup that put this patient in the ED.

Knowledge Check Before Any Insulin, Anywhere In any DKA patient, a potassium below 3.3 mmol/L before starting insulin means you should: Start insulin at a higher rate to correct the acidosis faster Start insulin, and add potassium to the same bag Hold insulin and replete potassium first No change — insulin doesn't affect potassium Insulin drives potassium intracellularly. Starting it on a patient who's already hypokalemic risks a fatal arrhythmia before the acidosis itself does any more harm. The Mental Checklist Before Insulin Before hanging any insulin infusion in DKA — this case or any other — the same three-item check runs every time: potassium (hold below 3.3), fluids already running, and a working diagnosis that actually accounts for the acidosis in front of you. It's a small, boring habit. It's also exactly the kind of habit that keeps a fixable metabolic problem from becoming an iatrogenic cardiac one.

What Was Actually Done Management Why This Order The sequence below isn't arbitrary. Insulin treats the ketoacidosis — the actual emergency — regardless of what the glucose reads, so it starts as soon as potassium is safe. The SGLT2 inhibitor gets stopped because it's the precipitant here, not an innocent bystander sitting on the med list. Everything after that is about making sure the insulin deficiency that started this doesn't get another chance. Insulin infusion started — treating the ketoacidosis , not the glucose number. Dapagliflozin SGLT2 inhibitor — blocks glucose reabsorption in the kidney, independent of insulin identified as the precipitant and discontinued indefinitely . Discharged on insulin glargine Long-acting basal insulin — covers background glucose needs between meals 40 units at night, insulin lispro Rapid-acting insulin — covers the glucose rise from meals 12 units with meals, plus metformin Biguanide — reduces hepatic glucose output; usually first-line for T2DM . Referred to endocrinology for close outpatient follow-up.

24 Hours Later Outcome Anion Gap 20 → 13 Triglycerides 2050 → 1400 mg/dL Clinical picture resolved on the insulin infusion, and she recovered fully. Notice what confirmed that: the anion gap closing, not the glucose — the same lesson that opened this case, now working in her favor. Glucose was never the variable that mattered here; it was the one that almost got everyone looking the wrong way.

Take-Home Teaching Points Strip away the specific numbers and this case reduces to four transferable habits — the kind worth carrying into the next shift, not just this diagnosis. A "normal" glucose doesn't clear a vomiting, tachypneic diabetic on an SGLT2 inhibitor — check a gap and ketones anyway. SGLT2 inhibitors should be held during acute illness, before surgery, and with reduced intake — see the glucose-lowering drugs lecture . Trend the anion gap and ketones, not the glucose, to follow resolution — see acute & chronic complications . Real labs have real snags — severe lipemia can block the exact test you need most, and that itself is information.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: The Patient 22F · Emergency Department Headache, polydipsia, and progressively worsening confusion. Background: morbid obesity (BMI 56.6), idiopathic intracranial hypertension managed with a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt A tube draining excess cerebrospinal fluid from the brain's ventricles to the abdomen, to relieve raised intracranial pressure and an occipital nerve stimulator, and months of supratherapeutic glucocorticoid dosing for a presumed inflammatory condition. High-dose glucocorticoids Steroid hormones (e.g. prednisone/hydrocortisone-class) — potent anti-inflammatories, but raise blood glucose and suppress the body's own cortisol production over time Tramadol (up to 450mg/day) A weak opioid agonist with serotonergic activity — this dose is well above the typical ceiling Tapentadol A dual opioid agonist / noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, used here for chronic pain Muscle relaxants Centrally-acting agents for chronic pain/spasm — can contribute to sedation or confusion in overdose or combination A shunt in her skull, months of steroids, and high-dose opioids — before any labs come back, this history alone means "confusion" can't be assumed metabolic. Hover the chips if a drug class doesn't ring a bell.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: How She Got Here The Lead-Up Four threads running in parallel — a shunt, a steroid taper problem waiting to happen, an opioid load, and now a metabolic derangement. Any one of them could explain "confusion" on its own. That's the actual difficulty of this case.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: On Arrival Vitals & Exam BP 180/120 HR 113 SpO₂ Normal GCS 15/15 Glucose (mg/dL) 583 Exam: alert and fully oriented at this moment (the confusion has been transient , not constant). No focal neurological deficits. Cushingoid features — centripetal obesity, violaceous striae, peripheral edema — visible evidence of the chronic steroid exposure. How an EM Physician Reads This 180/120 is a hypertensive emergency-range reading, not a rounding error. In isolation it might just be pain and anxiety. In a patient with a VP shunt and a history of transient confusion, it also has to make you think about intracranial pressure — and a fingerstick glucose of 583 doesn't automatically explain that BP away. The move here isn't "pick the metabolic story or the neurosurgical story." It's carry both until one is ruled out.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Checkpoint Before Any Labs Come Back Take thirty seconds and actually write something down — the exercise only works if you commit to an answer first. A VP-shunted patient on chronic steroids and high-dose opioids presents with headache and transient confusion. What's on your differential? Compare against a broad differential Worth having on the list: shunt malfunction / raised intracranial pressure, intracranial hemorrhage, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) or DKA, opioid toxicity or withdrawal, steroid-induced psychosis, and — easy to forget precisely because she's on steroids — adrenal crisis if a dose was missed. A high glucose on the monitor doesn't let you skip the neurosurgical half of this list.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Knowledge Check HHS vs. DKA Which combination is most classically associated with HHS rather than DKA? Glucose > 250 mg/dL, pH < 7.3, prominent ketosis Glucose < 200 mg/dL, high anion gap, positive ketones Glucose usually > 600 mg/dL, osmolality > 320, minimal-to-absent ketosis Normal glucose, low bicarbonate, elevated lactate HHS trades the dramatic acidosis of DKA for a dramatically higher glucose and osmolality — there's usually just enough residual insulin to suppress ketogenesis, but nowhere near enough to control glucose. That's exactly why HHS patients often look "less sick" on a blood gas while being just as dangerous — arguably more, since HHS actually carries a higher mortality rate than DKA.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Lab Interpretation First Bloodwork Glucose 583 mg/dL (32.4 mmol/L) · measured Na⁺ 135 mmol/L · K⁺ 4.6 mmol/L · HbA1c Glycated hemoglobin — reflects average blood glucose over the prior ~3 months 9.9%. What Actually Jumps Out An HbA1c of 9.9% with no prior diabetes diagnosis is itself a clue: this glucose didn't spike in the last few hours, it's been climbing for months — tracking almost exactly with how long she's been on high-dose steroids. The measured sodium of 135 looks unremarkable at a glance; it's the corrected value that tells the real story, because severe hyperglycemia pulls water out of cells and dilutes serum sodium, masking real free-water loss.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Approach & Review Reading Any Suspected Hyperosmolar Panel The systematic read for any severely hyperglycemic patient, DKA or HHS. 1 Never trust the raw sodium at extreme glucose levels. Hyperglycemia osmotically pulls water into the vascular space, diluting sodium — the raw number understates true free-water deficit. 2 Correct the sodium before you interpret it. Classic correction: add 1.6 mmol/L to sodium for every 100 mg/dL glucose above 100 (some now use 2.4 as a more physiologically accurate factor at very high glucose). 3 Calculate (or estimate) osmolality. 2×Na⁺ + glucose/18 + urea/2.8 (SI units). Above ~320 mOsm/kg is the classic HHS threshold, and correlates with mental status change. 4 Check for ketones anyway. Even in a picture that looks like "pure" HHS, mixed DKA/HHS pictures exist — don't assume they're mutually exclusive. 5 Match the correction rate to the risk. Whatever the number, don't fix it too fast — rapid osmolality shifts risk cerebral edema, especially in a patient whose brain is already unhappy.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Checkpoint Do the Correction Yourself Measured Na⁺ is 135 mmol/L. Glucose is 583 mg/dL. Using the classic factor (+1.6 mmol/L per 100 mg/dL glucose above 100), what's the corrected sodium? Check (583 − 100) / 100 × 1.6 = 7.73. 135 + 7.73 = 142.7 mmol/L — solidly within the normal range, despite the raw value sitting at the low end. This is the whole point of correcting it: the "normal-looking" raw sodium was actually hiding a real free-water deficit that the correction reveals.

entries.t: The Detail That Names the Disease
entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Lab Interpretation The Detail That Names the Disease C-peptide A byproduct made in equal amounts to a person's own (endogenous) insulin — a marker of how much insulin the pancreas itself is still producing 5.77 ng/mL (elevated) · urine ketones ++/+++ · serum ketones absent · mild transaminitis · neutrophilic leukocytosis. Elevated C-peptide plus severe hyperglycemia, with urine ketones positive but serum ketones absent, points most toward: Absolute insulin deficiency (type 1 diabetes / severe DKA) Preserved insulin production overwhelmed by severe insulin resistance A lab error — these findings are contradictory Alcoholic ketoacidosis A high C-peptide means her pancreas is still pumping out insulin — the problem isn't supply, it's that steroid-driven insulin resistance has overwhelmed it. The urine ketones are a mild, nonspecific finding (can reflect fasting/dehydration); the absent serum ketones are the more reliable negative — together they argue against true ketoacidosis and for HHS.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Knowledge Check The One People Underestimate Compared to DKA, mortality in HHS is: Higher — often cited around 10–20%, versus <5% for DKA Lower, since there's no significant acidosis About the same in most series Zero if glucose is corrected within 24 hours HHS patients tend to be older with more comorbidities, and the profound dehydration and hyperosmolality do real damage on their own, acidosis or not. The absence of dramatic blood gas findings can make HHS feel like the "less scary" cousin of DKA — the mortality data says otherwise.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Working It Up Ruling Out the Shunt Non-contrast CT brain: no hemorrhage, no abnormal parenchymal densities, no midline shift, normal ventricles. CT angiography/venography: no acute intracranial pathology, no venous thrombosis. No clinical or radiologic evidence of shunt malfunction — imaging quality was partly limited by artifact from the neuromodulation device. Why Image At All, Given the Glucose It's tempting to skip imaging once a glucose of 583 is sitting in front of you — it's such a satisfying explanation. But she has a VP shunt and a headache, and shunt malfunction can be rapidly fatal if missed. The metabolic explanation being likely is not the same as it being confirmed , and the cost of being wrong here is enormous. Image first, then let the metabolic workup do the rest of the explaining.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Approach & Review Working Up Any Undifferentiated Confusion The framework this whole case is really testing — useful on every altered patient, not just this one. 1 ABCs and a fingerstick glucose, immediately. Before anything else — glucose is the fastest reversible cause to catch or exclude. 2 Take a focused history for red flags. Hardware (shunts, pacemakers), medications (opioids, steroids, anticoagulants), and the tempo of onset (sudden vs. gradual) all narrow things fast. 3 Do a real focused neuro exam. Focal deficits push you toward structural causes; a symmetric, non-focal exam pushes toward metabolic/toxic/infectious ones — but doesn't rule structural out. 4 Sort causes into buckets, and work more than one. Structural, metabolic, toxic, infectious, and endocrine causes aren't mutually exclusive — a patient can have hardware and a metabolic derangement at the same time. 5 Don't let the most convenient explanation close the workup. The most dangerous bucket (structural) is exactly the one it's easiest to talk yourself out of checking once a metabolic number looks bad enough.

entries.t: Why You Can't Just Stop the Steroids
entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Mechanism Why You Can't Just Stop the Steroids Two consequences of the same chronic exposure now pull in opposite directions: the steroid is driving her glucose up, but her body has also become dependent on it to avoid adrenal crisis Life-threatening cortisol deficiency — hypotension, shock, and collapse when the body can't mount its own stress response . (See the approach to endocrine disease lecture for the HPA axis this hinges on, and diabetes pathophysiology for insulin resistance.)

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Knowledge Check Beyond This Case Glucocorticoids raise blood glucose primarily by: Directly destroying pancreatic beta cells Blocking glucose absorption in the gut, forcing compensatory overproduction Increasing hepatic gluconeogenesis and inducing peripheral insulin resistance Increasing renal glucose reabsorption Unlike SGLT2 inhibitors (which lower glucose by blocking renal reabsorption) or sulfonylureas (which force insulin release), steroids push glucose up through the liver and muscle/fat tissue — the pancreas isn't the problem, which is exactly why her C-peptide is high, not low.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: What Was Actually Done Management Why Slow and Careful She already had one episode of transient encephalopathy from this metabolic state — correcting it too fast risks triggering cerebral edema, the same danger taught with rapid correction in pediatric DKA. Everything here moves deliberately: fluids and insulin bring the glucose and osmolality down gradually, while the steroid dose comes down on a schedule measured in days, not a single stop. Aggressive isotonic fluid resuscitation, plus IV insulin, titrated to avoid too-rapid correction. Electrolytes monitored and repleted through treatment. Glucocorticoids continued , not stopped — high-dose IV hydrocortisone tapered gradually over a 13-day course. Transient bacteremia identified and treated per culture sensitivities — infection was likely a contributing precipitant.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Checkpoint Naming the Risk Her ACTH and morning cortisol both came back suppressed. If her steroids were simply stopped today instead of tapered, what specific endocrine emergency is she now at risk of? Check Months of exogenous steroid have told her hypothalamus and pituitary to stop signaling for cortisol, and her adrenal glands have atrophied from disuse. Pull the exogenous source away suddenly and there's no cortisol reserve to fall back on — the result is hypotension, shock, and collapse. It's the same HPA-axis suppression driving her hyperglycemia that now makes the "obvious" fix (stop the drug) dangerous.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Outcome What Happened Mental Status Transient confusion → Full recovery Steroid Dose High-dose IV → Tapered over 13 days Full neurologic recovery with no new imaging findings. Discharged on basal insulin (glargine) plus correctional rapid-acting insulin, with close endocrinology and neurology follow-up to manage both the diabetes risk and the ongoing steroid taper.

entries.p: Daily Case: HHS & the Steroid Trap
entries.x: Take-Home Teaching Points Strip away the specific numbers and this case reduces to habits worth carrying into the next shift. A high glucose is a reason to test the metabolic hypothesis, not a reason to stop testing the others — especially with neurosurgical hardware in the picture. HHS trades DKA's dramatic acidosis for a dramatically higher glucose and osmolality, and is arguably the more dangerous of the two. Correct sodium before you interpret it at extreme glucose levels — the raw number can hide a real free-water deficit. Chronic steroids can cause the very hyperglycemia in front of you and simultaneously make abruptly stopping them dangerous — see the approach to endocrine disease lecture .

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back A real ED presentation, worked through step by step — from an ambiguous drowsy patient, through an incomplete initial response to treatment, to the pharmacology and labs that explain why. Dotted, colored terms — like this — show a quick definition on hover or tap.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: The Patient 78M · Found at Home His wife finds him unusually drowsy at lunchtime — slurred, slow to respond, not himself. She calls an ambulance. Background: early-stage Alzheimer's dementia A progressive neurodegenerative disease affecting memory and executive function — relevant here because he manages his own medications and type 2 diabetes with, by his family's account, good long-term control. Metformin 1g twice daily An insulin sensitizer — on its own, essentially never causes hypoglycemia Gliclazide 40mg daily A sulfonylurea — stable dose for 7 years per his chart Two medications, stable for years. Nothing here looks dangerous on paper — which is exactly why what happens next is worth paying attention to.

entries.t: Before You See a Single Number
entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Knowledge Check Before You See a Single Number In a patient who manages his own diabetes medications but has early dementia, which drug carries the highest risk of a dangerous, prolonged low blood sugar if a dose gets accidentally doubled? Metformin Sitagliptin (a DPP-4 inhibitor) Gliclazide (a sulfonylurea) Empagliflozin (an SGLT2 inhibitor) Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors, and SGLT2 inhibitors essentially never cause hypoglycemia on their own — they don't force insulin release independent of glucose. Sulfonylureas do exactly that, which makes them one of the few oral diabetes drugs genuinely dangerous in overdose. (More on the mechanism and the rest of this drug family in the glucose-lowering drugs lecture .)

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: On Arrival Vitals & First Glucose BP 136/76 HR 88 Mental Status Drowsy Glucose (mmol/L) 2.1 Glucose (mg/dL) 38 Vitals are otherwise unremarkable — this isn't sepsis, isn't a stroke picture, isn't a toxidrome. The capillary glucose is the one number that explains everything else on this panel. How an EM Physician Reads This "Check a glucose" on any altered patient isn't a formality — it's often the single fastest reversible cause you can catch or exclude in under a minute, before imaging, before most labs. Here it's not subtle: 2.1 mmol/L (38 mg/dL) is well into the range that causes exactly the drowsiness his wife described.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: First Response Initial Correction The ambulance crew give 250mL of IV 10% dextrose en route. By the time he reaches the ED, he is more alert and speaking normally, and his capillary glucose has corrected. Taken on its own, this looks like a straightforward hypoglycemic episode that has already been treated.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Clinical Course Recurrent Hypoglycemia Despite Treatment Despite a continuous dextrose infusion (uptitrated from 5% at 125mL/hr to 10% at 100mL/hr) and glucagon on top of it, he keeps dipping back below 3.5 mmol/L, hour after hour, in the resuscitation room.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Checkpoint Why Isn't This Working? How an EM Physician Reads This A single hypoglycemic episode that corrects with dextrose and stays corrected is one story. Recurring hypoglycemia despite an active dextrose infusion is a different story entirely — it means something is still actively pushing insulin out of his pancreas, faster than you can pour sugar in. Turning the dextrose rate up further is treating the symptom, not the driver. The question stops being "how do we raise his glucose" and becomes "what do we do to make his own insulin stop being the problem."

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Lab Interpretation Confirming the Cause Venous pH 7.41 Lactate (mmol/L) 2.3 Renal Function Normal Urine Sulfonylurea Screen Positive Venous pH reference range is roughly 7.35–7.45, so 7.41 is normal. Lactate's reference range is approximately 0.5–2.2 mmol/L, so 2.3 mmol/L is only marginally above it. Renal function is normal, and a urine sulfonylurea screen returns positive . Reading This Panel A normal pH with only a marginally elevated lactate argues against a primary metabolic acidosis or significant tissue hypoperfusion — this is not sepsis or shock driving the clinical picture. The mild lactate elevation is more consistent with the adrenergic stress response to hypoglycemia itself (catecholamine-driven glycogenolysis) than with a separate acid-base process. Normal renal function means reduced drug clearance is not compounding the picture. The positive sulfonylurea screen is the one result that actually confirms the mechanism, rather than simply being consistent with it.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Knowledge Check What This Panel Rules Out A normal venous pH with only a mildly elevated lactate (2.3 mmol/L, reference 0.5–2.2) in this setting most likely reflects: Early sepsis A catecholamine-driven stress response to hypoglycemia itself, not a separate acid-base process Alcoholic ketoacidosis Tissue hypoperfusion from cardiogenic shock Severe hypoglycemia triggers a counter-regulatory adrenergic surge, which can mildly raise lactate through glycogenolysis and increased glycolytic flux, independent of any perfusion or infectious process. The distinguishing feature is the normal pH: a lactic acidosis significant enough to explain a sick patient would be expected to lower it, not leave it untouched.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Checkpoint Naming the Move His urine screen confirms gliclazide on board. Recurring hypoglycemia despite an active dextrose infusion means his pancreas is still being forced to secrete insulin. What drug directly suppresses that ongoing insulin secretion — rather than just adding more glucose to outrun it? Check Octreotide , a somatostatin A hormone that broadly inhibits secretion across the body — growth hormone, insulin, glucagon, and several GI hormones analog, is now considered first-line adjunct therapy for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia — it acts directly on the beta cell to shut off insulin release, which dextrose alone cannot do.

entries.t: Working Up Recurrent or Refractory Hypoglycemia
entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Approach & Review Working Up Recurrent or Refractory Hypoglycemia A generalizable framework — not specific to sulfonylureas, useful for any patient whose sugar won't stay up. 1 Confirm Whipple's triad. Symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia, a low measured glucose at the time, and resolution of symptoms once glucose is corrected — all three, not just a low number on a machine that might be wrong. 2 Rule out exogenous causes first. Insulin, sulfonylureas, alcohol, and certain fluoroquinolone antibiotics are the most common and most directly treatable causes — check the medication list before chasing anything rarer. If the cause isn't obvious from history, a confirmatory panel drawn during the hypoglycemic episode — insulin, C-peptide, beta-hydroxybutyrate, and a sulfonylurea screen — can distinguish exogenous insulin (low C-peptide) from sulfonylurea or insulinoma (high C-peptide, only the former screen-positive). 3 If exogenous causes are excluded, think endogenous. Insulinoma, adrenal insufficiency, hypopituitarism, severe liver or kidney failure, sepsis, and non-islet-cell tumors can all drop glucose without any drug on board. 4 Match your monitoring window to the drug, not the symptoms. Feeling better after one correction doesn't mean the drug's effect is over — some agents keep stimulating insulin release for well past the point a patient looks and feels fine. 5 Have a plan beyond "more dextrose." If glucose keeps dropping despite adequate replacement, that's your cue to add a drug that suppresses insulin secretion rather than just outrunning it.

entries.t: Why More Sugar Can Feed the Problem
entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Mechanism Why More Sugar Can Feed the Problem Two inputs converge on the same channel: the drug forces it shut, and every dose of dextrose hands the beta cell more raw material to keep responding. Octreotide works because it acts downstream of the sulfonylurea entirely — it doesn't matter how much gliclazide is still bound.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Knowledge Check Beyond This Case Why is octreotide, rather than just more dextrose, considered definitive treatment for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia? It speeds up renal clearance of the sulfonylurea It suppresses ongoing beta-cell insulin secretion, independent of the sulfonylurea still being bound It raises blood glucose directly, the same way glucagon does It reverses the sulfonylurea's binding to its receptor Octreotide doesn't displace the drug or clear it faster — it acts on a completely separate receptor pathway to shut off insulin exocytosis from the beta cell. That's exactly why it works regardless of how much sulfonylurea is on board or how long it's expected to keep acting.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Management Octreotide Given, Glucose Stabilizes 50 micrograms of octreotide are given subcutaneously. His glucose stabilizes, and with hourly monitoring there are no further hypoglycemic episodes. The presentation, medication history, and the lab panel already reviewed were sufficient to confirm the cause — what remained was a management problem: suppressing ongoing insulin secretion for as long as the drug stayed active.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Checkpoint One More Thing to Justify Take a moment before revealing the answer. His glucose has been stable for hours after octreotide. Why keep him in hospital for 48 hours rather than discharging him once he looks and feels normal? Compare against a model answer Feeling fine is not the same as the drug being gone. Gliclazide can keep stimulating insulin release well past the point symptoms resolve, and a single dose of octreotide wears off over several hours too — so the real risk window is defined by the sulfonylurea's duration of action, not by how he feels right now. Discharging early on the strength of "he seems okay" is exactly how a patient bounces back with another hypoglycemic episode at home, this time with no one watching.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Outcome Before and After Glucose Stability Recurrent drops despite dextrose → Stable after octreotide Home Medications Metformin + gliclazide → Gliclazide stopped He's discharged home after 48 hours of observation. Gliclazide is discontinued, and he's referred to the diabetes team — both to reassess his regimen for something safer given his dementia, and to loop in family for medication supervision going forward.

entries.t: Why Early Discharge Would Have Been Unsafe
entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Take-Home Why Early Discharge Would Have Been Unsafe Clinical Teaching Point Had his wife not been present when the recurrence occurred at home, or had the team discharged him once his first dextrose bolus corrected his glucose, a subsequent episode could easily have gone unwitnessed. This case illustrates a management principle more than a diagnostic one — the cause was already clear from the history and confirmed on the sulfonylurea screen. The risk was in underestimating how long that cause would keep acting, not in identifying it. Recurrent hypoglycemia despite adequate dextrose means something is still actively driving insulin release — treat the driver, not just the number. Octreotide suppresses insulin secretion directly and is now first-line adjunct therapy for refractory sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia. Match the observation period to the drug's expected duration of action, not to how quickly symptoms resolve. Cognitive impairment plus self-administered medication is its own risk factor, independent of the specific drug — medication reconciliation and family involvement are part of the actual treatment plan.

entries.t: One More Drug Class to Know
entries.p: Daily Case: The Hypoglycemia That Kept Coming Back
entries.x: Knowledge Check One More Drug Class to Know Besides sulfonylureas and exogenous insulin, which of the following can also cause drug-induced hypoglycemia through a similar beta-cell K-ATP channel-blocking mechanism? Atorvastatin Certain fluoroquinolone antibiotics (e.g. levofloxacin, gatifloxacin) Amlodipine Levothyroxine Certain fluoroquinolones — gatifloxacin most notoriously, levofloxacin less commonly — can block the same pancreatic K-ATP channel sulfonylureas target, triggering unexpected hypoglycemia, occasionally severe enough to need octreotide too. Worth remembering the next time an antibiotic is on the medication list of a patient with unexplained low sugar.

entries.x: T + 0:00 Triage 45F · Severe Abdominal Pain Emergency Department · Triage Note Presenting Severe abdominal pain with repeated nausea and vomiting for 12 hours. No diarrhoea. History Intermittent abdominal pain for 10 days. Ankle swelling for 5 days. Background Thin-built farm labourer. Chronic smoker. No regular medications, no drug use. Past / family Non-contributory. No known thyroid, cardiac or liver disease. Notably absent No fever. No recent weight loss reported. entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Checkpoint Before Any Results Commit to an answer before revealing — the exercise only works if you actually decide. A thin 45-year-old with 12 hours of severe abdominal pain and vomiting, absent bowel sounds, HR 130 and BP 90/60. What are you working up, and what are you worried about? Compare against a broad differential Reasonable list: bowel obstruction, perforation, mesenteric ischaemia, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, and — given the hypotension and tachycardia — sepsis from an intra-abdominal source. Absent bowel sounds plus shock physiology makes a surgical abdomen the front-runner for almost everyone. That is the correct initial read. Hold onto how reasonable it feels; the rest of this case is about what that reasonable read costs.

entries.t: When the Labs Don't Match the Story
entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Approach & Review When the Labs Don't Match the Story A generalizable habit, not specific to this case: what to do when results arrive that your working diagnosis cannot explain. 1 Sort each abnormal result into "explained" or "unexplained" by your current diagnosis. Do this explicitly. Obstruction explains the urea and the leucocytosis. It does not explain a bilirubin of 6, an INR of 6.49, or a glucose of 60. 2 Count the unexplained findings. One outlier is noise. Three unexplained abnormalities spanning different organ systems is a second diagnosis announcing itself. 3 Ask what single process could produce all of them at once. Jaundice + coagulopathy + hypoglycaemia together point at the liver failing, or at a systemic state driving the liver to fail. Neither is a bowel problem. 4 Treat the unexplained findings as a reason to re-examine, not just to re-test. The most valuable next move is usually going back to the patient, not ordering another panel.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Knowledge Check Reading the Combination Unexplained jaundice, a markedly raised INR, and persistent hypoglycaemia occurring together most specifically indicate: Biliary obstruction from gallstones Pre-renal failure from vomiting and dehydration Failure of hepatic synthetic and metabolic function Haemolysis from an intra-abdominal infection Clotting factors are made in the liver, so a soaring INR that isn't from warfarin is a synthetic-function failure. Hepatic glycogen stores and gluconeogenesis defend the fasting glucose, so persistent hypoglycaemia points the same way. Obstruction would raise bilirubin but not the INR to 6.49 or drop the glucose. Each finding alone has a long differential — together they name the organ.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 0:30 Working diagnosis Treated as a Gut Problem The documented working diagnosis: intestinal pathology — gut infection, obstruction, or perforation. Management was conservative and symptomatic: Ranitidine H2-receptor antagonist — reduces gastric acid secretion Hyoscine butylbromide Antispasmodic — relaxes smooth muscle for colicky abdominal pain Ondansetron 5-HT3 antagonist antiemetic 50% dextrose 30 mL Given for the glucose of 60 mg/dL, then followed by a dextrose-saline infusion How an EM Physician Reads This Every one of these orders is defensible. The pain is treated, the vomiting is treated, the low glucose is corrected. Notice what the dextrose does though: it makes the most alarming number on the panel go away without anyone having to explain why a 45-year-old was hypoglycaemic in the first place. That is how anchoring actually operates in practice. Not as a wrong decision, but as a series of individually correct decisions that quietly close the question.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 4:00 Acute deterioration Four Hours In After four hours of observation she becomes anxious and restless , and complains of palpitations and shortness of breath. HR 170 BP 110/72 SpO₂ (room air) 86% Rhythm Irregular 12-lead ECG: atrial fibrillation with a fast ventricular response. No P waves; the R–R intervals are irregularly irregular against a wavering baseline.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 4:05 Arterial blood gas The Gas Arterial Blood Gas · room air Critical values Test Result Flag Reference pH 6.95 LL 7.35–7.45 PaCO₂ 46 H 35–45 mm Hg PaO₂ 77 L 80–100 mm Hg Bicarbonate 12 L 22–26 mmol/L Lactate 4.8 H 0.5–2.2 mmol/L Ionised calcium 0.74 LL 1.1–1.3 mmol/L Glucose 60 L 70–130 mg/dL Sodium / potassium 135 / 3.5 — 135–145 / 3.5–5.0 What Jumps Out A pH of 6.95 is barely compatible with life. The bicarbonate of 12 and lactate of 4.8 say this is a severe metabolic acidosis, and the PaCO₂ of 46 says something worse: she is not compensating. A patient with this degree of acidosis should be blowing off CO₂ hard, driving the PaCO₂ into the twenties. A "normal-ish" CO₂ here means respiratory failure on top of the acidosis. And the glucose is 60 again — despite dextrose four hours ago. The finding that was made to go away has come back.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Knowledge Check Beyond This Case A patient has a pH of 6.95 with a bicarbonate of 12 mmol/L. Their PaCO₂ is 46 mm Hg. What does that PaCO₂ tell you? Appropriate respiratory compensation is occurring Compensation is failing — a normal-range CO₂ is inappropriately high here and signals impending respiratory arrest There is a primary respiratory alkalosis alongside the metabolic acidosis The sample is venous rather than arterial In a metabolic acidosis this severe, expected compensation (Winter's formula: PaCO₂ ≈ 1.5 × HCO₃ + 8 ± 2) predicts a PaCO₂ around 26 mm Hg . Measuring 46 means she is retaining nearly twice the CO₂ she should be — the respiratory muscles are losing. This is one of the most dangerous patterns in emergency medicine precisely because the number sits inside the normal reference range and does not get flagged.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 4:15 Airway · the hinge of the case Found During Intubation Diltiazem 12.5 mg IV brought the rate from 170 to 130. But her GCS Glasgow Coma Scale — 15 is fully alert; 8 or below generally mandates a definitive airway fell to 9/15 (E2 V2 M4), and she was intubated. The Detail That Changes Everything While positioning her neck for intubation, the team noticed a 2 × 3 cm swelling in the front of her neck. Not found on the triage exam. Not found in four hours of observation. Found because someone finally had their hands on her neck, extending it, at hour four — during a procedure being done for a different reason entirely. Neck ultrasound: a thyroid nodule , heterogeneous, with increased vascularity on colour Doppler. An urgent thyroid profile was sent.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Checkpoint Re-read the Whole Case Every finding so far, with one new fact: there is a thyroid abnormality. Tachycardia 130 → AF with RVR at 170. Unexplained jaundice. Agitation then falling consciousness. Pedal oedema. Vomiting and abdominal pain. Persistent hypoglycaemia. A vascular thyroid nodule. Name the unifying diagnosis. Check Thyroid storm — decompensated thyrotoxicosis. It is a genuine multi-system mimic: it can present as an acute abdomen, as sepsis, as heart failure, as delirium, or as liver failure. In this patient it presented as all of them at once, which is exactly why it took four hours and an unrelated procedure to find.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Approach & Review Score It Yourself The Burch–Wartofsky Point Scale is how thyroid storm is recognised at the bedside — before any thyroid result returns. Work through her documented findings and tally it. Burch–Wartofsky Point Scale Pick the band matching her findings in each category. Temperature — she was normothermic Normothermic 0 100–100.9°F 10 102–102.9°F 20 ≥ 104°F 30 CNS — agitated and restless, then GCS 9 Absent 0 Mild — agitation 10 Moderate — delirium, extreme lethargy 20 Severe — seizure, coma 30 GI–hepatic — vomiting, abdominal pain, bilirubin 6.0 Absent 0 Moderate — diarrhoea, nausea, pain 10 Severe — unexplained jaundice 20 Heart rate — 130/min at presentation 90–109 5 110–119 10 120–129 15 130–139 20 ≥ 140 25 Heart failure — pedal oedema for 5 days Absent 0 Mild — pedal oedema 5 Moderate — bibasilar rales 10 Severe — pulmonary oedema 15 Atrial fibrillation — present at T+4:00 Absent 0 Present 10 Precipitant history — likely gut infection Negative 0 Positive 10 0 0 of 7 categories scored Her documented score was 85 (20 jaundice + 20 tachycardia + 5 pedal oedema + 10 atrial fibrillation + 20 mental status + 10 precipitant). A score ≥ 45 is highly suggestive of thyroid storm regardless of how the thyroid numbers look — the scale is deliberately built from bedside findings so it can be applied before any assay returns. Note that she scored 0 for temperature: she was afebrile throughout. Waiting for fever would have meant never scoring her at all.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 5:30 Thyroid profile Confirmation Thyroid Function Urgent Test Result Flag Reference TSH < 0.00005 LL 0.35–5.5 µIU/mL T4 150.69 H 57–148 nmol/L T3 4.20 H 1.54–3.08 nmol/L Worth Noticing A completely suppressed TSH with raised T4 and T3 — primary hyperthyroidism, exactly the pattern in the thyroid function algorithm . But look at how modest the hormone elevations are. T4 of 150.69 against an upper limit of 148 is barely abnormal. This is the single most important lab lesson in thyroid storm: the severity of the storm does not track the height of the hormone levels. Storm is a clinical diagnosis about decompensation, not a threshold on an assay. A patient can die with a T4 that a lab would flag as only marginally high.

entries.t: Treating Thyroid Storm: Why the Order Matters
entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Approach & Review Treating Thyroid Storm: Why the Order Matters A generalizable framework. Each step blocks a different point in the pathway, and one ordering error can make the patient worse. 1 Block the adrenergic effects — beta-blocker (propranolol). Most of what is killing the patient acutely is catecholamine-driven. Propranolol also blunts peripheral T4→T3 conversion. Withhold if hypotensive or in cardiogenic shock. 2 Block new hormone synthesis — a thionamide (PTU or methimazole). PTU is generally preferred in the acute storm because it also blocks peripheral T4→T3 conversion: T3 falls roughly 45% in 24 hours with PTU versus 10–15% with methimazole. 3 Block hormone release — iodine, but only ≥ 1 hour AFTER the thionamide. This is the ordering trap. Iodine is substrate for hormone synthesis. Give it before the synthesis pathway is blocked and you fuel the fire you are trying to put out. 4 Block peripheral conversion — glucocorticoids. Hydrocortisone or dexamethasone. Also covers the relative adrenal insufficiency that accompanies severe thyrotoxicosis. 5 Treat the precipitant, and support everything else. Infection, fluids, cooling, electrolytes. The storm rarely arrives without a trigger, and it will not settle while the trigger is untreated.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: Knowledge Check One More Trap Which of the following is specifically avoided in thyroid storm? Hydrocortisone Propranolol Cholestyramine Aspirin Aspirin displaces thyroid hormone from thyroid-binding globulin, raising the free hormone fraction — the opposite of what you want. It is a genuinely easy error, because the reflex in a tachycardic, agitated, febrile-looking patient is to reach for an antipyretic. Use paracetamol/acetaminophen instead. Cholestyramine is a legitimate adjunct: it interrupts enterohepatic recycling of thyroid hormone.

entries.t: What the Team Could Actually Give
entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 5:30 → 12:00 ICU management What the Team Could Actually Give Step What happened here Beta-blocker Withheld. By this point HR had fallen to 60 and BP was 86/40 — she had moved from hyperdynamic to cardiogenic shock. Thionamide Methimazole 20 mg via nasogastric tube. PTU was not available in the hospital. Iodine Not given — the team judged multi-organ failure too advanced. Glucocorticoid Dexamethasone 8 mg IV, then 4 mg six-hourly. Circulatory support Noradrenaline, then dobutamine 10→20 µg/kg/min. Echo: EF 35% , cardiac output 2.6 L/min, dilated left ventricle. Note how the textbook sequence collapses under real constraints: the first-line drug was unavailable, the first-line beta-blocker was contraindicated by the time the diagnosis was made, and the patient was too unstable for the third step.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Abdomen That Wasn't the Problem
entries.x: T + 12:00 Outcome Torsades, and Then She developed torsades de pointes A polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting axis, characteristically precipitated by a long QT and by low magnesium, potassium or calcium . Magnesium sent at that moment returned at 0.7 mmol/L . She was given MgSO₄ 2 g over 5 minutes, then 5 g over 6 hours. She died approximately 8 hours after ICU admission — about 12 hours after she first walked into the emergency department with abdominal pain. On Reporting a Death The authors published this case precisely because it went badly. Thyroid storm carries a 20–30% mortality even when recognised promptly, and this patient arrived already in multi-organ failure — jaundiced, coagulopathic, hypoglycaemic. It is genuinely unclear that an earlier diagnosis would have saved her. What is clear is narrower and more useful: for four hours, nobody had a reason to touch her neck. That is the part worth carrying forward.

entries.x: Sim Lab Get It Into Your Units Your lectures work in mmol/L; this chart is in mg/dL. Convert first, then correct for albumin — because a raw total calcium means nothing until you know the albumin. Live converter — calcium mg/dL → mmol/L (× 0.2495): mg/dL = mmol/L His albumin is 4.1 g/dL , which is 41 g/L . Using the formula from lecture 2.2 — corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin) — what is his corrected calcium in mmol/L ? Check 15.1 mg/dL × 0.2495 = 3.77 mmol/L . Then 3.77 + 0.02 × (40 − 41) = 3.77 − 0.02 = 3.75 mmol/L . Note how little the correction moved it — his albumin is normal, so there was nothing to correct for. The correction matters when albumin is abnormal; here it simply confirms the number is real. Either way he is far above the > 3 mmol/L threshold at which lecture 2.2 says admit.

entries.t: What Does a Number This High Tell You?
entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Knowledge Check What Does a Number This High Tell You? A corrected calcium of 3.75 mmol/L, by itself, tells you which of the following? That this is primary hyperparathyroidism — it is the commonest cause overall That this is malignancy — only cancer raises calcium this high That he needs admission and treatment now, but nothing yet about the cause That the sample is haemolysed and should be repeated before acting Severity and etiology are separate questions. The height of the calcium drives urgency — above 3 mmol/L he is admitted regardless of cause — but it does not name the diagnosis. Very high values do shift the odds toward malignancy, and primary hyperparathyroidism is the commonest cause of hypercalcemia overall, but neither is established by a number alone. One test settles it, and it isn't the calcium.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Sim Lab Your Move: Find the Mechanism He is admitted, fluids are running. Now you need the cause. Order the workup. Investigation order set · etiology One of these splits the entire differential in half. The rest are downstream of it. The calcium axis PTH $ PTHrP $$ 25-OH vitamin D $ Other SPEP / light chains $$ 24-hour urine FeCa $$ Parathyroid sestamibi scan $$$ Imaging Chest X-ray $ Run selected tests PTH — 4.2 pg/mL (9.0–73.0) — suppressed PTHrP — 83 pg/mL (11–20) — markedly elevated 25-OH vitamin D — not elevated; no evidence of vitamin D excess SPEP / light chains — no monoclonal protein detected 24-hour urine FeCa — a test for distinguishing FHH from primary hyperparathyroidism. Both are PTH- mediated . With a suppressed PTH this question does not arise. Parathyroid sestamibi — localises a parathyroid adenoma. Only useful once PTH tells you the parathyroids are the problem. Chest X-ray (PA) — extensive bilateral nodular opacities , concerning for metastatic disease

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Interpretation PTH 4.2 — Suppressed Why This Single Value Ends Half the Differential His parathyroids are behaving correctly . Faced with a calcium of 3.75 mmol/L, a normal gland shuts off — and his has, to 4.2 against a floor of 9.0. That single result eliminates every PTH-mediated cause at once: primary hyperparathyroidism, tertiary hyperparathyroidism, and familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia all require a PTH that is high or inappropriately normal. Which means the calcium is coming from somewhere the parathyroids don't control — and the branch he has landed in is where malignancy lives. Follow the fork from lecture 2.2 : suppressed PTH → PTH-independent → exclude malignancy first, because it is the most time-critical cause on that list.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Checkpoint Name the Mechanism His PTHrP comes back at 83 pg/mL against a reference of 11–20. Name the protein — and, if you can, the syndrome it produces. Check PTHrP — parathyroid hormone-related peptide — producing humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy (HHM) . A tumour secretes it systemically; it binds the same PTH receptor that PTH does, so it drives bone resorption and renal calcium retention exactly as PTH would. But the assay for PTH doesn't detect it, so measured PTH stays appropriately suppressed by the hypercalcemia it is causing. PTHrP accounts for the majority of malignancy-associated hypercalcemia. It is the mechanism behind the PTHR being "shared with PTHrP" in Thyroid & Parathyroid Physiology .

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Knowledge Check Beyond This Case Why is PTH suppressed rather than elevated in humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy, even though PTHrP is acting on the PTH receptor? PTHrP destroys the parathyroid glands The parathyroids respond normally to the high calcium and shut off; the PTH assay does not cross-react with PTHrP PTHrP is converted into PTH in the circulation, so the two cannot be separated Tumour cells consume circulating PTH Two separate facts have to hold at once. Physiologically the glands are healthy and doing exactly the right thing — sensing a very high calcium through the calcium-sensing receptor and switching off. Analytically the immunoassay is specific for PTH and does not pick up PTHrP. So the hormone driving the hypercalcemia is invisible on the PTH result, and what you see instead is appropriate suppression. That is precisely what makes a suppressed PTH such a useful pointer rather than a confusing one.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Day 1 Finding the source Where Is It Coming From? The chest film prompts cross-sectional imaging. Imaging Contrast CT · MRI · bone scan CT abdomen Left renal mass, 5.5 × 5.0 × 5.3 cm, lobulated, heterogeneously enhancing — consistent with renal cell carcinoma. Left renal vein thrombus, presumed tumour thrombus. CT chest Multiple pulmonary nodules with central necrosis; mediastinal invasion from left upper lobe deposits. CT adrenal Enhancing right adrenal nodule. MRI brain Multiple enhancing lesions with vasogenic edema — frontal, parasagittal, parietal, masticator space, and two in the tongue and floor of mouth. entries.t: The Bone Scan Detail Is the Point
entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Mechanism The Bone Scan Detail Is the Point Humoral, Not Structural It would be intuitive to assume a widely metastatic cancer raises calcium by eating through bone. His scan argues otherwise — no widespread osteoblastic metastases , yet a calcium of 3.75 mmol/L. That is the distinction between the two malignant mechanisms in lecture 2.2. Local osteolytic hypercalcemia needs tumour physically in bone dissolving it, classically breast cancer and myeloma. Humoral hypercalcemia needs no bone involvement at all — a tumour anywhere secretes PTHrP into the circulation and the skeleton releases calcium on command from a distance. His tumour is in his kidney; his calcium is coming from his whole skeleton at once. Paraneoplastic hypercalcemia occurs in roughly 17% of renal cell carcinoma and marks aggressive disease.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Sim Lab Your Move: Sequence the Treatment Corrected calcium 3.75 mmol/L, creatinine 1.81, clinically dehydrated. Build the acute plan in the order you would actually do it — click to place, click a placed step to remove it. IV zoledronic acid 4 mg IV normal saline — restore volume Definitive: treat the underlying tumour Check order Volume first, always. Hypercalcemia causes a nephrogenic-DI-like polyuria, so these patients arrive volume-depleted — and a depleted kidney cannot excrete calcium. Saline both dilutes the calcium and restores the filtration that clears it. His creatinine of 1.81 is largely that dehydration. Then the bisphosphonate. Zoledronic acid shuts down osteoclast-mediated resorption, which is the tap PTHrP has turned on — but it takes 2–4 days to work, so it is never the thing that rescues the first few hours. Then the actual disease. Everything above is symptomatic. In humoral hypercalcemia the calcium only stays down if the tumour driving it is treated. Note what is not in this plan: a loop diuretic. Furosemide appears in the classic teaching sequence but only after full rehydration — given to a dry patient it worsens the depletion and the hypercalcemia. This patient was rehydrated and given zoledronate without it.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: What Was Actually Done The Real Sequence Volume: 3 litres of 0.9% saline as boluses, then a continuous infusion at 150 mL/hr for two days. Antiresorptive: zoledronic acid 4 mg IV. Oncological: pembrolizumab 200 mg IV every 3 weeks plus lenvatinib 20 mg orally daily — checkpoint inhibition with a tyrosine kinase inhibitor, the current standard for advanced RCC. Palliative: dexamethasone and radiation to the cerebral lesions. Calcium (mg/dL) 15.1 → 14.6 → 13.5 at discharge At 4 months Primary shrinking, lung mets regressing, cerebral edema improved

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Knowledge Check Read the Discharge Number He leaves hospital with a calcium of 13.5 mg/dL — still well above normal. What does that best reflect? Treatment failure — the zoledronic acid did not work A laboratory error, since bisphosphonates normalise calcium within hours Expected — the driver is still secreting PTHrP, so calcium falls only partly until the tumour itself is treated That he should have received a loop diuretic instead of saline Saline and a bisphosphonate act on the consequences — volume and bone resorption. Neither touches the tumour that is still releasing PTHrP into his circulation every hour. A partial fall is exactly what you should predict, and it is why the oncological treatment is the definitive calcium treatment rather than an afterthought. Expecting a normal calcium at discharge here would mean misunderstanding what is driving it.

entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Approach & Review Working Up Any Hypercalcemia The generalisable sequence — reusable on every hypercalcemic patient, not just this one. 1 Confirm it is real. Repeat the calcium and correct for albumin. Roughly 40% of total calcium is protein-bound, so an abnormal albumin makes the raw number lie in either direction. 2 Grade the urgency separately from the cause. Corrected calcium above 3 mmol/L, or any neurological or cardiac features, means treat now — before you know why. 3 Measure PTH. This is the branch point. High or inappropriately normal → PTH-mediated. Suppressed → PTH-independent. Every subsequent test depends on which side you land, which is why ordering the downstream tests first wastes them. 4 If PTH-independent, look for malignancy first. It is the most time-critical cause. PTHrP for humoral hypercalcemia, imaging for a primary, SPEP and light chains for myeloma, and consider vitamin D excess and granulomatous disease. 5 Treat the cause, not only the number. Fluids and bisphosphonates buy time. In a humoral picture the calcium is only fixed when the tumour is.

entries.t: What This Case Is Really About
entries.p: Daily Case: The Number That Was Never Going to Be the Diagnosis
entries.x: Take-Home What This Case Is Really About Clinical Teaching Point He had none of the classic renal cell carcinoma triad — no haematuria, no flank pain, no palpable mass. What he had was malaise, a few pounds of weight loss, and one abnormal number on a basic panel. The metabolic derangement was the presentation. This is the argument for checking a calcium in vague constitutional illness. It is a cheap, additive test on a panel you were already sending, and it is occasionally the only visible edge of something large. The height of the calcium sets the urgency; PTH sets the diagnosis. A suppressed PTH in hypercalcemia is not confusing — it is the parathyroids behaving correctly, and it points you straight at the PTH-independent causes. Humoral hypercalcemia needs no bone metastases at all. A normal bone scan does not exclude malignant hypercalcemia. Fluids first, then antiresorptive, then the tumour — and expect only a partial fall until the last of those happens.
